summary: The Open Mobile Alliance defines a Push-to-talk over Cellular service that uses SIP for half-duplex media sessions and instant messages. This informational document defines a SIP event package and data format for publishing, subscribing to, and being notified about extra capabilities that service requires.

eli5.summary: Walkie-talkie service on phones needs to share certain settings. This defines a way for devices to post those settings and get updates when they change.

questions: sip event package for push-to-talk over cellular
what is the sip poc-settings event package
subtitle: A SIP event package that lets push-to-talk phones publish their answer and barring settings so the network can react faster.

tldr.problem: Push-to-talk over Cellular needs very fast session setup and must avoid wasting scarce radio capacity, but the network does not know whether a called terminal is set to auto-answer, barring sessions or alerts, or able to handle several sessions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SIP event package poc-settings and an XML format, application/poc-settings+xml, so a terminal can publish four settings and network servers can subscribe to them and receive notifications.
tldr.outcome: A network server can answer sooner or filter requests on the user's behalf. The package is meant for PoC and the RFC says it may not be applicable to the general Internet.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No more than once every five seconds per user (SHOULD NOT exceed)

today: RFC 4354 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It says the package is applicable to the PoC service and may not be applicable to the general Internet.

sections.title: Why PoC Needs Settings
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) specifies the Push-to-talk over Cellular (PoC) service, where a SIP User Agent starts a session to one or more other User Agents, usually when the user pushes a button. OMA's requirements are stringent: the time from pressing the button to the indication to speak must be minimized, and unneeded traffic must be kept off the air interface.

Four user settings matter to the network:

  • Answer Mode (AM): Auto-Answer plays media as soon as it arrives, Manual-Answer alerts the user first.
  • Incoming Session Barring (ISB): the terminal accepts no incoming PoC sessions.
  • Instant Personal Alert Barring (IPAB): the terminal accepts no Instant Personal Alerts.
  • Simultaneous PoC Sessions Support (SSS): whether more than one PoC session at a time is accepted.

Knowing these lets a network server buffer media so the caller can speak before the called terminal answers, skip needless alerts, and decide whether to act as a B2BUA or a SIP proxy.
sections.eli5: The network wants to know if your phone is set to answer by itself, to ignore calls, or to take many calls. Knowing this saves time and radio space.

sections.title: The poc-settings Event Package
sections.content:
The package builds on SIP event notification (RFC 3265) and event publication (RFC 3903). A PoC terminal acts as an Event Publication Agent (EPA) and sends PUBLISH requests with its settings. A network server acts as an Event State Compositor (ESC), and as notifier tells subscribers when the settings change. The package name, used in the Event header field, is poc-settings, and it defines no extra Event parameters.

A SUBSCRIBE normally has no body; its Request-URI identifies the user. The default subscription expiration is 3600 seconds, and the subscriber MAY ask for another in the Expires header field. Notifiers SHOULD NOT send notifications for one user more than once every five seconds. There is no rate limit for publication, since changes are triggered by a human.

Only a single dialog is allowed from an initial SUBSCRIBE. Several terminals may be logged in for one user, and changes made at one apply to all of them, so each terminal is RECOMMENDED to subscribe to its own settings. When EPAs conflict, the ESC either composes a combined view or sends each terminal's settings so the subscriber can resolve it. The composition policy itself is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The phone posts its settings, the network server keeps them, and anyone allowed to ask can sign up to hear about changes, though not more than once every five seconds.

sections.title: The PoC-Settings Document
sections.content:
The data format is an XML document with MIME type application/poc-settings+xml. It MUST be well-formed, SHOULD be valid, and MUST be UTF-8 encoded XML 1.0. Its namespace is urn:oma:params:xml:ns:poc:poc-settings, and the root element is <poc-settings>.

Inside are zero or more <entity> elements, each with a required id attribute that is a globally unique identifier for an address of record representing an EPA. An EPA SHOULD include a single entity. An ESC may include several when it cannot resolve conflicts, or none when no publication has happened. Each entity holds up to one of each setting element:

  • <isb-settings> with <incoming-session-barring active=...>
  • <am-settings> with <answer-mode> set to automatic or manual
  • <ipab-settings> with <incoming-personal-alert-barring active=...>
  • <sss-settings> with <simultaneous-sessions-support active=...>

If simultaneous sessions support is false, a terminal already in a PoC session declines a second invitation. If it is true, the terminal will possibly accept it. Unknown elements and attributes from other namespaces MUST be ignored, which keeps the format extensible. The RFC also includes the XML Schema that implementations MUST comply with.
sections.eli5: The settings are written on a small form with four yes-or-no style boxes. If a form has a box you do not know, you skip it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Settings can reveal private information, so notifiers MUST authenticate all subscription requests (using SIP mechanisms from RFC 3261) and MUST NOT accept a subscription without the user's authorization. Servers receiving PUBLISH SHOULD authenticate the publisher.

Notification bodies can be encrypted and integrity-protected with S/MIME. Since the notifier may not hold the user's key, the NOTIFY SHOULD be signed by an authority over the user's domain.

The RFC gives attack examples. An outsider who learns a terminal is on automatic answer could send a malicious session with inappropriate media that plays automatically. One who learns it accepts simultaneous sessions could try to exhaust the User Agent with bogus sessions. Without integrity protection, a man-in-the-middle could alter notifications, which is annoying but not harmful.
sections.eli5: Knowing that a phone plays messages by itself could let a bad person send it a nasty message. So the network only tells the settings to people who are allowed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers the poc-settings event package and the MIME type application/poc-settings+xml. The MIME registration lists an optional charset parameter with a default of UTF-8, and its intended usage is limited use, restricted to PoC terminals and servers. The change controller is the Open Mobile Alliance, PoC working group.
sections.eli5: The new package name and file type were added to the official list so everyone uses the same names.

data.title: PoC-settings document
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<poc-settings xmlns="urn:oma:params:xml:ns:poc:poc-settings">
  <entity id="do39s8zksn2d98x">
    <isb-settings>
      <incoming-session-barring active="true"/>
    </isb-settings>
    <am-settings>
      <answer-mode>automatic</answer-mode>
    </am-settings>
    <ipab-settings>
      <incoming-personal-alert-barring active="false"/>
    </ipab-settings>
    <sss-settings>
      <simultaneous-sessions-support active="true"/>
    </sss-settings>
  </entity>
</poc-settings>

items.title: ISB
items.text: Incoming Session Barring: no incoming PoC sessions accepted.

items.title: IPAB
items.text: Instant Personal Alert Barring: no incoming alerts accepted.
